title: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck
note: DB titles (tr 'Özgür Olmak', de 'Frei sein', es 'Ser libre') are not faithful titles; the en DB title is the real one. Full text not read; facts come from Kindle highlights, Goodreads quotes, chapter listings and summaries. Confidence capped at medium.

facts.claim: Chapter 2, 'Happiness Is a Problem', has a section 'Choose Your Struggle'. Kindle highlights: 'What pain do you want in your life? What are you willing to struggle for?' and 'The relevant question is, "What pain do you want to sustain?"'
facts.source: Kindle highlights (elie.net); library catalog table of contents

facts.claim: Highlight: 'Everything worthwhile in life is won through surmounting the associated negative experience.'
Book notes: the people who enjoy the stresses and uncertainties of the starving-artist lifestyle are the ones who ultimately live it and make it.

Manson illustrates 'choose your struggle' with his own long fantasy of being a rock star: he dreamed of the stage for years but never did the work it required, because he wanted the result and not the process.
facts.source: One summary ('his own story of trying to become a rock star'); wording not verified

facts.claim: Chapter 5: the responsibility/fault fallacy. Some problems are not our fault, yet we are still responsible for them. Example: you wake up and find a newborn on your doorstep; it isn't your fault, but you must decide what to do, and you own the results of that choice.

Fault is about choices already made; responsibility is about the choices you are making now. Highlight: 'we, individually, are responsible for everything in our lives' and 'Accepting responsibility for our problems is thus the first step to solving them.'
facts.source: Kindle highlights; Goodreads/secondary paraphrase for the past/present wording

facts.claim: William James: around 1872 his life was falling apart and he considered taking his own life. One night, reading lectures by the philosopher Charles Peirce, he decided on a one-year experiment: believe he was 100 percent responsible for everything that occurred in his life and do everything to change his circumstances; if nothing improved, he would accept he was powerless. He later called this his rebirth.
facts.source: Goodreads quote from the book; Manson's own blog; StoryShots summary (1872, rebirth)

facts.claim: Chapter 6: 'You're Wrong About Everything (But So Am I)'. Growth is an endlessly iterative process; certainty is the enemy of growth.
Manson's Law of Avoidance: 'The more something threatens your identity, the more you will avoid it.'

Section 'How to Be a Little Less Certain of Yourself' poses three questions: 'What if I'm wrong?', 'What would it mean if I were wrong?', 'Would being wrong create a better or a worse problem than my current problem, for both myself and others?'
facts.source: Goodreads reader notes; Goodreads quote pages

facts.claim: Manson: if you believe you know everything you won't learn anything; accepting your ignorance is where learning begins.

Chapter 2 sections include 'Happiness Comes from Solving Problems'. Manson's point: problems never disappear, they are traded or upgraded; summaries give the example of an entrepreneur who escapes a boss's demands only to answer to investors.

rejected.claim: 'Why do athletes train six hours a day?' and 'why do some people stay in hard relationships?' as Manson's questions.
'The great majority of people who want the result but not the process never reach it.'
Manson quotes Viktor Frankl on choosing one's response in the camps.
rejected.reason: No source ties Frankl to this chapter of the book.

rejected.claim: Quotes 'Taking responsibility is not weakness, it is the only door to power' and 'You may not always control what happens...'
rejected.reason: Paraphrases presented as quotes; not found.

rejected.claim: Alcohol, overwork and compulsive relationships are all attempts to suppress uncertainty; learning to sit with uncertainty makes them unnecessary.
'The people with the most rigid views grow least; the most flexible learn most.'
